text:
customer_ops_taylor: Hey team — AcmeCorp's private control plane connections started failing around 11:05 UTC. They see TLS errors on client side during mTLS handshake. Error from app logs: 'tls: handshake failure (alert 40)'. Can we triage?

maya: thanks — can you paste the client logs + a short repro? which region? did this start after any cert rotation? :eyes: 

customer_ops_taylor: region: us-west-2, Private control plane v1.8. No cert rotation on our side. App logs show repeated 'handshake failure' and then immediate reconnect. Only affects their VPC peered subnets. Other customers fine.

devon: quick checks — can you run an openssl s_client from a host inside their VPC to our control plane IP and include -msg and -showcerts? also tcpdump of the ClientHello if possible.

customer_ops_taylor: ran these, pasting outputs clipped for thread.

--- begin: openssl s_client output ---
CONNECTED(00000003)
depth=2 O = AcmeCorp Root CA, CN = acme-root
verify return:1
depth=1 C = US, O = AcmeCorp Intermediate, CN = acme-intermediate
verify return:1
depth=0 CN = cp.acme.internal
verify return:1
SSL_connect:before/accept initialization
<<< TLS 1.3, Handshake, ServerHello
...
SSL_connect:SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL in connection to cp.acme.internal:443
write:errno=104
--- end ---

devon: hm write errno=104 usually means connection reset. Do you have a tcpdump of the TLS handshake?

customer_ops_taylor: yes — capture shows ClientHello followed by a short TLS Alert: 40 (handshake_failure). Packet sizes look truncated in one direction. snippet: 

14:11:05.123456 IP 10.1.2.3.52345 > 10.0.0.5.443: Flags [P.], seq 1:513, ack 1, win 64240, length 512
14:11:05.123789 IP 10.0.0.5.443 > 10.1.2.3.52345: Flags [R.], seq 1, ack 513, win 0, length 0

netops_jin: That seq/len pattern looks like clienthello fragmentation or MTU blackhole. What MTU on their VPC ENIs? Also check any egress NGFW rewriting.

customer_ops_taylor: ENI MTU = 9001. No changes reported on customer side. They do have an egress F5 that performs TLS inspection for outbound traffic. It might be touching traffic to our control plane IP.

eng-sre-lin: F5 TLS inspection often strips/interposes cert chains or rewrites SNI. If the F5 terminates TLS and re-initiates to us, and doesn't forward client certs or OCSP, mTLS will break. Can you confirm if the F5 is in full proxy mode for that destination IP?

customer_ops_taylor: Confirmed: F5 is in full-proxy SSL_FORWARDING for that outbound ACL. They said "we only inspect egress to unknown domains" but cp.acme.internal resolves to a CNAME that goes to our cloud endpoint; maybe it triggered the inspect rule.

security-ella: two potential failure modes: 1) the proxy terminates TLS and doesn't forward client certs (so server sees no client cert) — should be explicit in our logs; 2) proxy rewrites cert chain (drops intermediate) so server's OCSP responder check fails or leaf cert mismatch. Any server-side logs?

devon: pulled control plane logs for those connection attempts. We see a client_hello from 10.0.0.5 (the F5) with SNI 'cp.acme.internal' but the presented client cert was a proxy cert (CN=F5-Proxy) — we then attempt to validate client cert chain, OCSP check to acme-ocsp.example.com times out and we return handshake_failure. Log excerpt: 

[2026-03-12T11:05:05Z] TLS: client cert presented CN=F5-Proxy, chain incomplete, OCSP responder acme-ocsp.example.com timed out -> handshake aborted

netops_jin: ocsp timeout — if their proxy is doing TLS termination and re-issuing a cert it may not include the real client OCSP stapled response or intermediate. Also some proxies rewrite the chain order which our runtime is strict about.

maya: can we reproduce by forcing a connection that bypasses the F5? Or ask customer to add an egress allowlist for our control plane IP for the peering subnet? 

customer_ops_taylor: temporary bypass tested: route traffic from one test host via NAT gateway that doesn't hit the F5 — handshake succeeds immediately. Command used: curl --resolve cp.acme.internal:443:10.0.0.5 https://cp.acme.internal/health --cert client.pem --key client.key -v

--- success response ---
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"status":"ok"}
--- end ---

eng-sre-lin: that confirms the proxy is the culprit. Long-term options: 1) customer must configure F5 to do TLS pass-through for our control plane IP/SNI, or 2) enable our control plane to accept proxied client certs (not ideal), or 3) customer allowlists OCSP responder and passes stapled responses.

security-ella: also check for CNAME-induced SNI mismatches — if their proxy rewrites destination or we see mismatched SANs that can cause a different cert to be served by the proxy. Ask them to verify DNS resolution chain: dig +short cp.acme.internal; dig +trace cp.acme.internal; check for CNAME to external host.

customer_ops_taylor: they have cp.acme.internal -> cp-ext.acme.net -> cp-ingress.vendor.net (CNAME to vendor). The F5 inspects based on cp-ext.acme.net rule.

devon: proposed repro steps for support playbook (short):
1) From a host behind the customer's F5, run:
   - openssl s_client -connect cp.acme.internal:443 -servername cp.acme.internal -showcerts -msg > sclient.log
   - tcpdump -s 0 -w tls.pcap host cp.acme.internal and reproduce a failing handshake
2) From a host that bypasses the F5 (NAT gateway/test route) run same openssl/curl for golden successful trace
3) Share sclient.log and tls.pcap with us + F5 admin config snippet for SSL_FORWARDING rules and any client-certificate insertion config
4) As workaround ask customer to add our control plane IP to egress passthrough list for the peered subnet and/or whitelist acme-ocsp.example.com IPs for outbound TCP/80/443 to allow OCSP responses

netops_jin: additional check: F5 may be truncating TLS extension list (ALPN, max_fragment_length) leading to unexpected handshake. Capture ClientHello raw bytes and compare. Use tshark: tshark -r tls.pcap -V -Y 'ssl.handshake.type==1' and inspect extension ordering.

customer_ops_taylor: forwarded F5 config to us. They have "insert-client-cert" set to true and "server-side-ocsp-disable" in the profile. Looks like they intentionally suppress OCSP to speed up egress. That breaks our server-side OCSP validation.

eng-sre-lin: if their proxy suppresses OCSP we should be tolerant: fallback to allow stapled responses or a grace-window for cached OCSP responses. But changing validation semantics is a product decision — will escalate to runtime team. For now advise customer to enable OCSP passthrough or allow our OCSP responder IPs.

support-bot: Incident created: INC-2026-0334 — assigned to eng-sre-lin, netops_jin, and customer_ops_taylor. Priority: P2.

security-ella: next steps for us:
- eng-sre-lin: review logs + propose safe runtime fallback (cache OCSP for 5m on proxied connections)
- netops_jin: prepare a short KB for customers with egress inspection proxies explaining required passthrough settings and commands to test
- customer_ops_taylor: coordinate with AcmeCorp to add our CP IP to F5 passthrough and test the prod path

customer_ops_taylor: AcmeCorp asked for a one-liner to verify passthrough quickly. Suggested: 
- From inside their VPC (before change): curl -v --cert client.pem --key client.key https://cp.acme.internal/health 2>&1 | sed -n '1,120p'
- After adding passthrough: repeat above, success should return HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

maya: update — AcmeCorp enabled passthrough for the test host, confirmed successful handshakes and healthy status. They'll schedule a full subnet change next maintenance window.

eng-sre-lin: I'll file a runtime follow-up ticket to consider more graceful handling for proxied client cert chains and OCSP suppression. Thanks all, closing thread once KB is posted. :white_check_mark:"
